passage: Tenzin, you asked why I made you delete that photo. Let me tell you about my college friend Neelam. She was clever and funny, and she posted everything: party photos, rants about professors, jokes that went a bit too far. We all laughed. Then, in her final year, she applied for a job at a big company. At the interview, the manager said, "We saw your posts about your professors." Neelam's face went white. She didn't get the job. She cried for days. Afterward, she spent a whole weekend cleaning her profiles, making her personal accounts private and creating a professional one. She got a good job six months later. But she said she never forgot that interview. Think before you post, beta.

qa.q: What did the manager say they had seen?
qa.a: They said they had seen Neelam's posts about her professors.

qa.q: Why did Neelam's face go white at the interview?
qa.a: She felt shocked and afraid, suddenly realising her old online rants were visible to employers and could cost her the job.

qa.q: What steps did Neelam take afterward, and why were they useful?
qa.a: She cleaned her profiles, made personal accounts private and built a professional one, so employers would see her best side.

qa.q: How might Tenzin feel after hearing this story?
qa.a: He might understand why the elder asked him to delete the photo and think more carefully before posting.

grounding: An elder tells a young person how a friend's posts affected a job interview and how she managed her online presence afterwards.

passage: Urmila had two days before her first big job interview, and her professional profile was almost empty. Worse, her old accounts were full of silly photos and a heated argument from two years ago. Her roommate Ganga looked her up and winced. "That argument is the third result." Urmila panicked. With the internet at the hostel going on and off, they worked late into the night: making personal accounts private, deleting the worst posts, adding her internship, project and volunteering to her professional page. Ganga took a clean photo of her against the hostel wall. "It's not perfect," Urmila said. "It's honest," Ganga replied. At the interview, the panel asked about her volunteering, not her argument. Urmila almost laughed with relief.

qa.q: What did the panel ask Urmila about at the interview?
qa.a: They asked about her volunteering.

qa.q: Why did Urmila panic when Ganga looked her up?
qa.a: She realised an old heated argument appeared near the top of her search results, where employers could easily see it.

qa.q: What made Urmila's clean-up effective under time pressure?
qa.a: She focused on the essentials: making accounts private, deleting the worst posts and adding real achievements to her professional page.

qa.q: How might Ganga feel after Urmila's interview?
qa.a: She'd likely feel relieved and proud to have helped, and glad her honest advice paid off. 🙂

grounding: It shows a young woman managing her digital footprint and professional profile under time pressure before an interview.

passage: Divyansh and Abhinav were final-year students in Chandigarh, sharing a room and a laptop charger. One evening, Abhinav was scrolling through his old posts. "Look at this," he said, showing a joke he'd made about a classmate in first year. "I thought it was funny then." Divyansh cringed. "Employers can see that." Abhinav frowned. "It's my personal account." "Personal isn't private," Divyansh said. "And your future partner's family might look too." Abhinav was quiet. That weekend both of them went through their profiles. Abhinav deleted the joke and messaged the classmate an apology. Divyansh updated his professional page with his project and a clear photo. "We look like adults," Abhinav joked. "Almost," Divyansh said.

'Sumit, beta, come here. Your cousin says companies look at these profiles?'

He sat down, suddenly quiet. 'I've got an interview at the bank on Friday.'

'So I'll go through everything tonight. Archive the silly stuff, make the account private, fix my work profile.'
'And the jokes about your professors?'
He winced. 'Those too.'
'Good.' She patted his head. 'Be yourself online, beta. Just the self you'd let me see.'

passage: When I was twenty, I posted a long rant about my internship manager. No name, but anyone could work out the company. It got likes, and I felt brave. Six months later, in a final-round interview, the panel asked me, very politely, how I handle disagreements with seniors. One of them had clearly seen the post. I stammered through an answer and didn't get the offer. My friend Lalit said, 'You're not wrong to be upset, Chaitanya, but that's the internet. It's a permanent room.' I deleted the post that night. Since then I've used a simple test: would I be fine with a future boss, or someone I'm dating, reading this? I still share opinions, mostly about my work and projects. The angry bits I say to friends, face to face.

qa.q: What did the panel ask Chaitanya in the final-round interview?
qa.a: How Chaitanya handles disagreements with seniors.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya's feelings about the post change between posting it and the interview?
qa.a: Chaitanya felt brave when the likes came in, but in the interview felt exposed and stammered, realising the post had followed along.

qa.q: What test does Chaitanya use now before posting?
qa.a: Whether it would be fine for a future boss or partner to read it, with angry venting kept for face-to-face talks with friends.

qa.q: How might the interview panel have seen the post?
qa.a: As a hint about how Chaitanya might treat a manager in public, which made them cautious even if the frustration was understandable.

grounding: A young adult looks back on how a public rant affected a job interview and how they now manage their digital footprint.

passage: Placement cell note, 10 August. Irawati (final-year commerce) came in for a profile review before campus interviews. Her professional profile was thin: no photo, one line saying "hardworking". Her public account, though, had four years of posts, including a sarcastic thread about a former teacher. She had heard from Chetan, a senior, that an interviewer last year asked him about a joke he posted in second year; he said it rattled him for the whole interview. Irawati spent an hour with me. She archived the thread, made her personal account private, and added two real projects to her profile: the college fest budget and a survey of local shopkeepers. She hesitated over deleting some funny posts: "That's me too." We agreed she could keep what is hers, as long as she would be comfortable explaining it. — Mrs Banerjee, placement officer

qa.q: What did Irawati add to her profile?
qa.a: Two real projects: the college fest budget and a survey of local shopkeepers.

qa.q: What does Irawati's hesitation over deleting funny posts suggest?
qa.a: Irawati felt torn between wanting to look professional and not wanting to erase parts of herself she enjoys.

qa.q: What rule did Mrs Banerjee and Irawati agree on, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: Keep posts that are hers if she would be comfortable explaining them, which balances honesty with a professional image.

qa.q: What was it like for Chetan when the interviewer asked about the old joke?
qa.a: It rattled Chetan for the whole interview, so he likely felt embarrassed and off balance, which is why he warned others.

passage:
Wednesday night
Searched my own name for the first time before sending the internship application. Big mistake. Or big good mistake? Result three: my old art account from Class 11, with a post calling a well-known design school "overrated and full of rich kids". Result five: a photo Anjali tagged me in at her birthday, me mid-sneeze, eyes shut 😅
The sneeze I can live with. The rant I can't. I don't even believe that anymore.
Anjali came over with chips and we went through everything. Deleted the rant, removed the tag (after asking; she laughed), and turned my art account into a proper portfolio: my best twelve drawings, dated, with a line on each about what I was trying.
Strange, looking at my past self the way a stranger would. Tomorrow I send the application. Nervous, but what they'll find now is actually me.
— Aadhya

qa.q: What did Aadhya's old post call the design school?
qa.a: Overrated and full of rich kids.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling on finding the old rant?
qa.a: Aadhya felt embarrassed and uneasy, because the rant no longer matches what Aadhya believes.

qa.q: How did turning the art account into a portfolio help?
qa.a: It replaced a random old footprint with twelve dated drawings and notes, showing growth to anyone who searches.

qa.q: How might Anjali have felt about removing the tag?
qa.a: Anjali laughed about it, so she seemed relaxed and happy to help, and being asked first probably felt respectful.

grounding: A diary shows a young person searching their own name before an application and cleaning up and curating their footprint.

passage:
Lakshmi, you asked about the worst interview moment of my life. It's this. I'm Mehak, and last year I had a final-round interview at a design firm.
Near the end, the interviewer smiled and said, "We saw your post about your last internship." My stomach dropped. Two years earlier, angry after a bad week, I'd written a long public rant calling that company "a circus run by clowns".
I didn't pretend. I said, "That was unfair and unprofessional. I was frustrated, but I should've raised it privately. I've learned from it." She nodded and moved on.
I didn't get that job. Maybe it wasn't the post. But the next week I went through ten years of my profiles. I deleted, made things private, and started posting only what I'd be happy for a future boss, or future partner, to read.

qa.a: Mehak felt a jolt of panic and embarrassment, stomach dropping.

qa.q: Which choice in the interview was wise, and why?
qa.a: Owning the post honestly instead of denying it, because it showed maturity even if the job didn't come through.

qa.q: How might the interviewer have seen Mehak's answer?
qa.a: The interviewer may have respected the honesty, even if the old rant still raised doubts.

passage:
I'm Tenzin. I shared a hostel room with Zubin in final year, and I saw him get serious about placements.
One night he sat with his laptop for three hours, scrolling back through his old posts, mouth moving as he read. Every few minutes he'd groan and hit delete: a party photo with someone passed out, a joke about a girl from his batch, a fight in the comments with a stranger.
Then he made a proper profile: clear photo, summary of his projects, links to his code. He asked me to pretend to be a recruiter and search his name. I found only one old thing, a comment on a cricket forum, harmless.
I can't say if he felt ashamed or just careful. But when he got his offer, he said, "The first thing they did was look me up." He wasn't smiling when he said it.

qa.q: What did Zubin link on his new profile?
qa.a: Links to his code.

qa.q: What does Zubin groaning at old posts suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests Zubin felt embarrassed and uncomfortable, seeing how the posts might look to strangers.

qa.q: What would you add to Zubin's clean-up for other students?
qa.a: Think about how posts affect the people in them too, like the passed-out friend, and pause before posting in future.

qa.a: She would likely have felt hurt and disrespected, which makes deleting it about more than placements.

Friday: The interviewer said, "I saw your bridge model online. Walk me through the load test." Hemant felt his shoulders relax. He talked for ten minutes without once looking at his notes.
